title: Short Stuff: Beulah Mae Donald
summary: Josh and Chuck tell the story of Beulah Mae Donald, whose 19-year-old son Michael Donald was lynched by Ku Klux Klan members in Mobile, Alabama, in 1981. Police were slow to act and at one point suggested a drug deal; Beulah Mae pushed for justice, the FBI got involved, and two men (Henry Hayes and James "Tiger" Knowles) were convicted of the murder. She then brought a civil suit against the United Klans of America as an organization, won a multimillion-dollar jury verdict that bankrupted the group, and additional clan members were later indicted, including Henry Hayes, who was executed in the electric chair, and Frank Cox, who was sentenced to 99 years. Beulah Mae forgave the killers, and Herndon Avenue was renamed in Michael's honor.

segments.title: Introduction to Beulah Mae Donald
segments.summary: Josh introduces the story of Beulah Mae Donald, who took on the Klan after her son was murdered, and notes the source article.

segments.title: Michael Donald's murder
segments.summary: Michael Donald, 19, was abducted, beaten, had his throat cut, and was hanged from a tree a few blocks from his home in Mobile, Alabama. The hosts describe the national shock and Beulah Mae keeping the casket open, and note a cross was burned at the Mobile County courthouse that night.

segments.title: Slow police response and the fight for justice
segments.summary: Police were slow to pursue the Klan and at one point suggested a drug deal. Beulah Mae was offended by the characterization of her son and pushed for action. Her friend, a district attorney, brought in the FBI, and two men, Henry Hayes and James Tiger Knowles, were convicted of the murder. The hosts say the killing was a random act driven by Klan anger over a jury verdict.

segments.title: Civil suit against the United Klans of America
segments.summary: Beulah Mae filed a civil suit with other plaintiffs against the Klan as an organization, arguing it deprived Black citizens of constitutional rights through intimidation and murder. Morris Dees and the Southern Poverty Law Center helped. Additional members, including Benny Jack Hayes and Frank Cox, were drawn in, and a jury awarded seven million dollars, which bankrupted the group.

segments.title: Aftermath, sentences, and legacy
segments.summary: Henry Hayes was executed in the electric chair, Frank Cox received 99 years, and Benny Jack Hayes died before his trial concluded. Knowles apologized at the civil trial and served about 25 years. Beulah Mae forgave the killers, and Herndon Avenue was renamed in Michael's honor. She died about a year and a half after the verdict.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts recommend a four-part series on the case and close the episode.
